questions.commandDemand: Give the mechanism. Say which way heat moves and why.
questions.stimulus: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon are placed in the same bowl of hot soup. After two minutes, the handle of the metal spoon feels hot but the handle of the wooden spoon does not.
questions.stem: Explain why the handle of the metal spoon feels hot, and explain why the wooden spoon's handle does not.

fuzzyTraps.precise: metal is a good conductor of heat, so heat energy is conducted along it

fuzzyTraps.vague: the heat goes up the spoon
fuzzyTraps.precise: heat energy is transferred from the hotter soup to the cooler handle

chain.text: The soup is hotter than the spoon, so heat energy flows from the soup to the spoon.
Metal is a good conductor of heat, so heat energy is conducted quickly along it.
The metal handle gains heat energy and its temperature rises, so it feels hot.
Wood is a poor conductor of heat, so very little heat energy is conducted to the wooden handle.

questions.modelAnswer: The soup is at a higher temperature than the spoon, so heat energy is transferred from the soup to the spoon. Metal is a good conductor of heat, so the heat energy is conducted quickly along the spoon to the handle. The handle gains heat energy and its temperature rises, so it feels hot. Wood is a poor conductor of heat, so very little heat energy is conducted along the wooden spoon, and its handle stays close to room temperature.
markPoints: Heat flows from the hotter soup to the cooler spoon
Metal is a good conductor of heat, so heat is conducted quickly along it
The handle gains heat energy so its temperature rises
Wood is a poor conductor of heat, so little heat energy reaches the wooden handle
questions.whyMarksLost: Both spoons are in the stem, so both need explaining. The direction of heat flow, from hotter to colder, is a mark on its own.

questions.commandDemand: Distinguish heat from temperature. The two words are not interchangeable.
questions.stimulus: A cup of hot water at 80 degrees Celsius and a bathtub of warm water at 40 degrees Celsius are placed in the same room.
questions.stem: Explain why the bathtub contains more heat energy than the cup, even though its temperature is lower.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the bath is bigger so it has more heat
fuzzyTraps.precise: the bath contains a much greater amount of water, so it contains more heat energy in total

fuzzyTraps.vague: temperature is how much heat there is
fuzzyTraps.precise: temperature is the degree of hotness, not the amount of heat energy

chain.text: Temperature measures how hot something is; heat energy is the total amount of energy it contains.
The bathtub contains a far greater amount of water than the cup.
Although each portion is cooler, the total heat energy in the bath is greater.

questions.modelAnswer: Temperature is a measure of how hot something is, while heat energy is the total amount of energy the water contains. The bathtub holds a much greater amount of water than the cup. Even though each part of the bath water is at a lower temperature, there is so much more water that the total heat energy contained in the bathtub is greater than that in the cup.
markPoints: Temperature is the degree of hotness; heat energy is the total amount of energy
The bath contains a much greater amount of water
So its total heat energy is greater even though each part is cooler
questions.whyMarksLost: This question exists to catch students who use heat and temperature as one word. The first mark is entirely about telling them apart.

questions.commandDemand: State the final state and give the reason using the direction of heat flow.
questions.stimulus: A metal block at 20 degrees Celsius is placed into a beaker of water at 70 degrees Celsius. The two are left together for a long time.
questions.stem: Predict what will happen to the temperature of the block and of the water, explain why, and state how you would know when the transfer of heat has stopped.

fuzzyTraps.precise: both will reach the same temperature

fuzzyTraps.vague: the cold goes into the water
fuzzyTraps.precise: heat energy is transferred from the hotter water to the cooler block

chain.text: The water is hotter, so heat energy flows from the water to the block.
The block gains heat energy and warms; the water loses heat energy and cools.
Transfer continues until both are at the same temperature.
Both readings stop changing and stay equal.

questions.modelAnswer: The temperature of the block will rise and the temperature of the water will fall. The water is at a higher temperature than the block, so heat energy is transferred from the hotter water to the cooler block. The block gains heat energy and becomes hotter, while the water loses heat energy and becomes cooler. This continues until both are at the same temperature. You would know the transfer had stopped when the two thermometer readings stayed the same as each other and no longer changed over time.
markPoints: Block's temperature rises and water's temperature falls
Heat energy is transferred from the hotter water to the cooler block
Transfer continues until both are at the same temperature
Heat transfer has stopped when both thermometer readings stay the same
questions.whyMarksLost: The end state is where most answers stop early. There is no heat transfer once there is no temperature difference, and saying how you would observe that is the fourth mark.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using expansion on heating.
questions.stimulus: A glass jar has a metal lid that is stuck. Running the lid under hot water makes it easier to open.
questions.stem: Explain why running the lid under hot water helps.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the metal lid gains heat energy and expands
the lid expands more than the glass, so the fit becomes looser

chain.text: The metal lid gains heat energy from the hot water.
The metal expands on heating.
The lid expands more than the glass jar, so it becomes looser and easier to turn.

questions.modelAnswer: The metal lid gains heat energy from the hot water. Metal expands when it gains heat energy. The lid expands more than the glass jar does, so the gap between the lid and the jar increases and the lid becomes looser, making it easier to turn and open.
markPoints: The metal lid gains heat energy and expands
The lid expands more than the glass, so it becomes looser
questions.whyMarksLost: The comparison is the second mark. Saying only that the lid expands does not explain why that loosens it; it must expand more than the jar.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a workable improvement and explain it using heat transfer.
questions.stimulus: A student builds a box to keep an ice cube from melting for as long as possible. Her first design is a thin cardboard box.
questions.stem: Suggest one improvement to her design, explain how it would work, and explain why the phrase keeping the cold in is not a correct description.

fuzzyTraps.precise: reduce the heat energy gained from the warmer surroundings

chain.text: Line the box with a thick layer of a poor conductor of heat.
This slows heat energy passing from the warmer surroundings into the ice.
The ice melts because it gains heat, not because cold escapes.

questions.modelAnswer: She could line the box with a thick layer of a poor conductor of heat, such as polystyrene or wool. The surroundings are warmer than the ice, so heat energy is transferred from the surroundings to the ice; a poor conductor reduces the rate at which this happens, so the ice gains heat energy more slowly and takes longer to melt. Saying the box keeps the cold in is not correct, because cold is not a thing that can move. What actually happens is that heat energy moves from the warmer surroundings into the ice, and the insulation slows that down.
markPoints: Add a thick layer of a poor conductor of heat
This reduces the heat energy gained from the warmer surroundings, so melting is slower
Cold does not move; heat energy moves from the warmer surroundings into the ice
questions.whyMarksLost: Examiners penalise the cold-moving model directly. The third mark is for stating the correct direction of heat flow.

questions.commandDemand: Read the graph description and state what it shows about the materials.
questions.stimulus:
Three identical containers of hot water were each wrapped in a different material and their temperatures recorded every five minutes for thirty minutes.

Material D: fell from 80 to 74 degrees Celsius
Material E: fell from 80 to 58 degrees Celsius
Material F: fell from 80 to 45 degrees Celsius
questions.stem: What can you infer about the three materials as conductors of heat?

fuzzyTraps.precise: D is the poorest conductor of heat

chain.text: The water wrapped in D cooled the least and the water in F cooled the most.
A smaller temperature drop means less heat energy was transferred to the surroundings.
D is the poorest conductor of heat and F is the best conductor of the three.

questions.modelAnswer: Material D is the poorest conductor of heat and Material F is the best conductor of the three. The water wrapped in D fell by only 6 degrees Celsius, showing that the least heat energy was transferred to the surroundings through it. The water wrapped in F fell by 35 degrees Celsius, showing that heat energy was transferred through it most quickly.
markPoints: D identified as the poorest conductor and F as the best conductor
Reason linked to the size of the temperature drop and heat transferred to the surroundings
questions.whyMarksLost: Calling D 'the best' is ambiguous, because best depends on the purpose. The examiner wants the scientific ranking as conductors of heat.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the effect of heat on the state of matter.
questions.stimulus: A beaker of ice is heated steadily and its temperature recorded. The temperature rises from -10 to 0 degrees Celsius, then stays at 0 degrees Celsius for several minutes while the ice melts, then rises again.
questions.stem: Explain why the temperature stays at 0 degrees Celsius for several minutes even though the beaker is still being heated.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the heat energy gained is used to change the state from solid to liquid
the heat energy is still gained, but it does not raise the temperature during the change of state

chain.text: The temperature stays constant at 0 degrees Celsius, which is the melting point of ice.
The heat energy gained is used to change the state from solid to liquid.
Because the energy goes into melting rather than raising temperature, the reading does not change until all the ice has melted.

questions.modelAnswer: Zero degrees Celsius is the melting point of ice. While the ice is melting, the heat energy gained from the heater is used to change the state of the water from solid to liquid rather than to raise its temperature. The temperature therefore stays constant at 0 degrees Celsius until all the ice has melted, after which the heat energy gained raises the temperature of the liquid water again.
markPoints: 0 degrees Celsius is the melting point of ice
The heat energy gained is used to change the state from solid to liquid
Not to raise the temperature, so the reading stays constant
The temperature rises again only after all the ice has melted
questions.whyMarksLost: Writing that the heat 'stops having an effect' is marked wrong. The energy is still being absorbed; it is doing a different job.

questions.commandDemand: Give the mechanism using how light travels.
questions.stimulus: A torch is shone at an opaque ball. A shadow of the ball appears on a screen behind it.
questions.stem: Explain how the shadow is formed, and explain why the shadow has the same shape as the ball.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the opaque ball blocks the light because light travels in a straight line
no light reaches that part of the screen, forming a shadow

chain.text: Light travels in a straight line.
The opaque ball blocks the light, which cannot bend around it.
The region receiving no light has the outline of the ball, so the shadow matches its shape.

questions.modelAnswer: Light from the torch travels in a straight line. The ball is opaque, so it does not allow light to pass through, and because light travels in straight lines it cannot bend around the ball. No light therefore reaches the part of the screen directly behind the ball, forming a shadow. The shadow has the same shape as the ball because the region of the screen that receives no light is bounded by the straight rays that just graze the edge of the ball, so it takes the outline of the object.
markPoints: The ball is opaque and blocks the light
Light travels in a straight line, so no light reaches the screen behind the ball
The blocked region has the outline of the object, so the shadow takes its shape
questions.whyMarksLost: Travels in a straight line is the phrase that separates AL1 from AL3 here; without it there is no reason light could not go around.

questions.commandDemand: State what happens to the shadow and give the reason.
questions.stimulus: A ball is held between a torch and a screen. The ball is then moved closer to the torch, while the screen stays where it is.
questions.stem: Predict what happens to the size of the shadow and explain why. Predict what would happen instead if the screen were moved away from the ball while the ball stayed still.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the shadow gets bigger because it is nearer
fuzzyTraps.precise: the ball blocks a larger portion of the light spreading from the torch

chain.text: The shadow becomes larger.
Light spreads out as it travels from the torch.
Closer to the torch, the ball blocks a wider portion of that spreading light.
Moving the screen back lets the blocked region spread further, so the shadow is larger again.

questions.modelAnswer: The shadow becomes larger. Light spreads out as it travels away from the torch, so when the ball is moved closer to the torch it blocks a larger proportion of the light leaving it, and a bigger area of the screen receives no light. If instead the screen were moved further away while the ball stayed still, the shadow would also become larger, because the region of blocked light continues to spread out as it travels, so it covers a bigger area by the time it reaches the screen.
markPoints: The shadow becomes larger when the ball moves towards the torch
Because the ball blocks a larger portion of the light spreading from the torch
Moving the screen further away also makes the shadow larger, as the light spreads further before reaching it
questions.whyMarksLost: The second case tests whether the spreading-light idea was understood or just memorised for one arrangement.

questions.commandDemand: Give the mechanism by which we see a non luminous object.
questions.stimulus: A student can see a red book on a table in a lit room. When the lights are switched off and the room is completely dark, she cannot see it at all.
questions.stem: Explain why she cannot see the book in a completely dark room, and explain why she can see a lit torch bulb in the same dark room.

fuzzyTraps.vague: there is no light to see
fuzzyTraps.precise: there is no light for the book to reflect into her eyes

fuzzyTraps.vague: the book has no light of its own
fuzzyTraps.precise: the book is non luminous, so it does not produce its own light

chain.text: The book is non luminous, so it does not produce its own light.
We see it because it reflects light into our eyes; in darkness there is none to reflect.
A bulb is luminous, so light from it travels straight to the eyes with no reflection needed.

questions.modelAnswer: The book is a non luminous object, which means it does not produce its own light. We are able to see it only because it reflects light from a source into our eyes. In a completely dark room there is no light for the book to reflect, so no light from the book enters her eyes and she cannot see it. A lit torch bulb is a luminous object: it produces its own light, which travels directly from the bulb into her eyes, so she can see it even when the room is dark.
markPoints: The book is non luminous and does not produce its own light
We see it only by light reflected off it into the eyes, and there is none to reflect
A lit bulb is luminous, producing its own light which travels directly to the eyes
questions.whyMarksLost: The contrast is the mark. Luminous and non luminous only mean something when set against each other.

questions.commandDemand: Use the results to classify each material and give the evidence.
questions.stimulus:
Four sheets were each placed between a torch and a screen. What appeared on the screen was recorded.

Sheet A: a bright patch of light, the object behind could be seen clearly
Sheet B: a dim patch of light, the object behind could not be seen clearly
Sheet C: a dark shadow, no light at all
Sheet D: a bright patch of light, the object behind could be seen clearly
questions.stem: Infer whether each sheet is transparent, translucent or opaque, and give the evidence for each.

fuzzyTraps.precise: B is translucent because it allows only some light to pass through and the object cannot be seen clearly

chain.text: All the light passes through and objects are seen clearly, so they are transparent.
Only some light passes through and objects cannot be seen clearly, so it is translucent.
No light passes through, so it is opaque.

questions.modelAnswer: Sheets A and D are transparent, because they allowed light to pass through and the object behind could be seen clearly. Sheet B is translucent, because it allowed only some light to pass through, producing a dim patch, and the object behind could not be seen clearly. Sheet C is opaque, because it did not allow any light to pass through and formed a dark shadow.
markPoints: A and D identified as transparent with evidence
B identified as translucent, with only some light passing through
And the object behind not being seen clearly as the deciding evidence
C identified as opaque, with no light passing through
questions.whyMarksLost: Translucent is decided by the object behind not being clearly visible, not merely by the patch being dimmer. That distinction is a mark.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a workable design and justify it with a property of light or materials.
questions.stimulus: A bedroom window faces a bright street lamp. The family wants the room dark at night but still bright during the day when the curtains are open.
questions.stem: Suggest a suitable material for the curtains and explain your choice. Explain also why a translucent material would not solve the family's problem.

fuzzyTraps.precise: an opaque material, which does not allow light to pass through

chain.text: Use an opaque material for the curtains.
An opaque material lets no light through, so the room stays dark.
Opening the curtains lets light through the transparent window glass.
A translucent material lets some light through, so the room would not be properly dark.

questions.modelAnswer: The curtains should be made of an opaque material. An opaque material does not allow any light to pass through it, so when the curtains are closed at night the light from the street lamp is blocked and the room stays dark. During the day the curtains can be opened, and light passes through the transparent glass of the window, so the room is bright. A translucent material would not solve the problem, because it allows some light to pass through it; the street lamp's light would still reach the room, only more dimly, so the room would not be properly dark.
markPoints: An opaque material chosen
It lets no light through, so the room is dark when the curtains are closed
Opening them lets light through the transparent window by day
A translucent material lets some light through, so the room would not be dark
questions.whyMarksLost: Translucent is the trap. It sounds like a compromise but it fails the actual requirement, and saying why is worth a mark.

questions.commandDemand: State what would be observed. No reasons needed, but be precise about the change.
questions.stimulus: A student places a straight pencil into a glass of water and looks at it from the side.
questions.stem: Describe what the student observes, and name the property of light that causes it.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the pencil appears bent or broken at the water surface
light changes direction as it passes from water into air

chain.text: The pencil appears bent or broken at the surface of the water.
Light from the pencil changes direction as it passes from the water into the air.
The part of the pencil under the water appears to be in a different position.

questions.modelAnswer: The pencil appears bent or broken at the point where it enters the water, although it is still straight. This happens because light travelling from the pencil changes direction as it passes from the water into the air, so the part of the pencil below the surface appears to be in a different position from where it actually is.
markPoints: The pencil appears bent or broken at the water surface, while remaining straight
Light changes direction when it passes from water into air
questions.whyMarksLost: Saying the pencil 'is bent' loses the mark. It appears bent; the pencil itself does not change. Precision about appearance versus reality matters here.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using how light behaves at a surface.
questions.stimulus: Road workers wear jackets with strips that shine brightly when a car's headlights fall on them at night.
questions.stem: Explain why these strips make the workers easier to see at night.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the strips reflect the light from the headlights
they are non luminous and only reflect light that falls on them

chain.text: Light from the car's headlights falls on the strips.
The strips reflect a large amount of this light back towards the driver.
More light enters the driver's eyes from the worker, so the worker is seen more easily.

questions.modelAnswer: Light from the car's headlights falls on the strips. The strips are made of a material that reflects a large amount of light back towards its source. More light from the worker therefore enters the driver's eyes than would come from ordinary clothing, so the worker appears brighter and is seen more easily.
markPoints: The strips reflect the light from the headlights
More light enters the driver's eyes from the worker
The strips are non luminous, so they only reflect and do not produce light
questions.whyMarksLost: Writing that the strips glow or light up shows the luminous distinction has not landed, and it is now worth a mark of its own.

questions.commandDemand: Give the mechanism from source to ear.
questions.stimulus: A student strikes a drum and hears a sound from across the room.
questions.stem: Explain how the sound reaches the student's ear, and state what would happen if the room were emptied of all air.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the drum skin vibrates when struck

fuzzyTraps.vague: the sound goes through the air
fuzzyTraps.precise: the vibrations travel through the air as sound

chain.text: The drum skin vibrates when it is struck.
The vibrations are passed on to the surrounding air and travel through it to the ear.
With no air there is nothing to carry the vibrations, so no sound is heard.

questions.modelAnswer: When the drum is struck, the drum skin vibrates. These vibrations are passed on to the air around the drum and travel through the air across the room to the student's ear, where they are detected and heard as sound. If the room were emptied of all air there would be no medium to carry the vibrations from the drum to the student, so no sound would be heard at all.
markPoints: The drum skin vibrates when struck
The vibrations travel through the air, a medium, to the ear
With no air there is no medium, so no sound would be heard
questions.whyMarksLost: Sound is not something the drum sends out. It is a vibration passed through a medium, and the medium has to be named.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and give the reason using what sound needs to travel.
questions.stimulus: An electric bell is placed inside a sealed glass jar. The air is gradually pumped out of the jar while the bell keeps ringing.
questions.stem: Predict what happens to the sound heard as the air is removed, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.precise: there are fewer air particles to carry the vibrations
sound needs a medium to travel through, and cannot travel through a vacuum

chain.text: The sound becomes fainter and eventually cannot be heard.
As air is removed there are fewer air particles inside the jar.
Sound needs a medium to travel through, so with almost no air the vibrations cannot be carried to the jar wall.

questions.modelAnswer: The sound becomes fainter and eventually cannot be heard at all. As the air is pumped out, there are fewer and fewer air particles inside the jar. Sound needs a medium to travel through, because it travels as vibrations passed from particle to particle. With almost no air left, there is nothing to carry the vibrations from the bell to the wall of the jar, so no sound is heard.
markPoints: The sound becomes fainter and eventually inaudible
As air is removed there are fewer particles to carry the vibrations
Sound needs a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum
questions.whyMarksLost: The word medium is what the mark scheme wants. Saying sound needs air is nearly right but misses that solids and liquids also carry it.

questions.commandDemand: Read the data and state what it shows, comparing the right pairs.
questions.stimulus:
A student tapped one end of a long rod and measured how loud the sound was at the other end, using rods of the same size made of different materials.

Steel rod: very loud
Wooden rod: loud
Air column, no rod: faint
questions.stem: What can you infer about how well sound travels through different materials? Support your answer with the results, and state which pair you compared.

fuzzyTraps.precise: sound travels best through steel, a solid, and least well through air, a gas

chain.text: The sound was loudest through steel and faintest through air alone.
Steel and wood are both solids, and both beat the air column.
Sound travels better through solids than through gases.

questions.modelAnswer: Sound travels better through solids than through gases. Comparing the steel and wooden rods with the column of air, the sound was very loud through the steel rod and still loud through the wooden rod, both of which are solids, but only faint through the air, which is a gas. Because both solids carried the sound better than the gas did, the pattern is about the state of the material rather than about steel in particular.
markPoints: Sound travels better through solids than through gases
Supported by comparing the steel and wooden rods with the air column
Both rods are solids and both carried the sound better than air
questions.whyMarksLost: Ranking the three materials is only half the answer. The conclusion should generalise to solids and gases, which is the pattern the data actually shows.

questions.commandDemand: Link the change made to the change in the sound, using pitch or loudness precisely.
questions.stimulus: A student plucks a guitar string, then tightens it and plucks it again with the same force.
questions.stem: Explain what happens to the pitch of the sound and why. State what the student would have to change instead to make the sound louder.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the pitch of the sound becomes higher
loudness and pitch are different; tightening changes the pitch

chain.text: The pitch of the sound becomes higher.
The tighter string vibrates faster when plucked.
Loudness depends instead on how much energy the vibration carries, so plucking harder makes it louder.

questions.modelAnswer: The pitch of the sound becomes higher. When the string is tightened it vibrates faster when plucked, and the faster an object vibrates the higher the pitch of the sound it produces. To make the sound louder rather than higher, the student would have to pluck the string harder. This gives the string a vibration that carries more energy, and the more energy the vibration carries, the louder the sound.
markPoints: The pitch becomes higher
The tighter string vibrates faster, and faster vibration gives higher pitch
To make it louder she would pluck harder, giving a vibration carrying more energy
questions.whyMarksLost: Pitch and loudness get mixed constantly. Tightening changes how fast it vibrates; plucking harder changes how much energy the vibration carries.

questions.commandDemand: State a similarity and a difference, referring to both in each point.
questions.stem: Compare pitch and loudness of a sound.

fuzzyTraps.vague: pitch is high and loudness is loud
fuzzyTraps.precise: pitch is how high or low a sound is; loudness is how soft or loud it is

chain.text: Both are properties of sound and both depend on the vibration of the source.
Pitch depends on how fast the object vibrates.
Loudness depends on how much energy the vibration carries.

questions.modelAnswer: Both pitch and loudness are properties of a sound and both depend on the vibration of the object producing it. However, pitch describes how high or low a sound is and depends on how fast the object vibrates, with faster vibration giving a higher pitch. Loudness describes how soft or loud a sound is and depends on how much energy the vibration carries, with more energy giving a louder sound.
markPoints: Similarity: both are properties of sound depending on the vibration of the source
Pitch depends on how fast the object vibrates
Loudness depends on how much energy the vibration carries
questions.whyMarksLost: Both definitions must reach back to the vibrating object. Defining them separately without that link is description, not science.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a practical solution and explain how it reduces the sound.
questions.stimulus: A family living beside a busy road finds the traffic noise inside their flat too loud.
questions.stem: Suggest two things the family could do to reduce the noise indoors, and explain how each would work.

fuzzyTraps.vague: put up thick curtains to stop noise
fuzzyTraps.precise: thick curtains absorb the sound, so fewer vibrations are passed on into the room

chain.text: Hang thick, heavy curtains over the windows.
Soft, thick materials absorb sound, so fewer vibrations pass into the room.
Close the windows, or fit double glazing.
This removes the direct air path, so fewer vibrations can travel through into the room.

questions.modelAnswer: The family could hang thick, heavy curtains over the windows. Soft and thick materials absorb sound, so fewer of the vibrations from the traffic are passed on into the room and the noise heard is softer. They could also keep the windows closed or fit double glazing. This removes the open air path through which the vibrations travel most easily, so fewer vibrations reach the inside of the flat.
markPoints: First workable suggestion
Its explanation linked to absorbing sound or blocking the path of vibrations
Second workable suggestion
Its own explanation, not a repeat of the first
questions.whyMarksLost: Two suggestions need two explanations. Writing one and saying 'the same for the other' leaves a mark on the table.

questions.commandDemand: State what would be observed at each step of the demonstration.
questions.stimulus: A student places some grains of rice on a stretched drum skin and then taps the drum.
questions.stem: Describe what happens to the rice grains, and explain what this shows about sound.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the rice jumps because of the noise
fuzzyTraps.precise: the rice jumps because the drum skin is vibrating

chain.text: The rice grains bounce and jump on the drum skin.
The drum skin is vibrating after being tapped.
This shows that sound is produced by a vibrating object.

questions.modelAnswer: The rice grains bounce and jump up and down on the drum skin. This happens because the drum skin is vibrating after it has been tapped, and the vibrating skin makes the grains move. This shows that sound is produced by an object that is vibrating.
markPoints: The rice grains bounce or move up and down
This shows that the drum skin vibrates, and that sound is produced by vibration
questions.whyMarksLost: The conclusion is the second mark. Describing the rice without saying what it proves answers only half the question.

questions.commandDemand: State the energy changes in order, using the form from and to.
questions.stimulus: A battery powered torch is switched on and the bulb lights up and becomes warm.
questions.stem: Describe the energy conversions that take place in the torch, and state which conversion is not useful.

fuzzyTraps.precise: chemical energy stored in the battery is converted into electrical energy
electrical energy is converted into light energy and heat energy

chain.text: Chemical energy stored in the battery becomes electrical energy.
In the bulb, electrical energy becomes light energy.
Some electrical energy becomes heat energy, which does not help the torch do its job.

questions.modelAnswer: The chemical energy stored in the battery is converted into electrical energy, which flows through the circuit. In the bulb, this electrical energy is converted into light energy, which is why the bulb lights up. Some of the electrical energy is also converted into heat energy, which is why the bulb becomes warm. That conversion is not useful, because the purpose of a torch is to produce light, not heat.
markPoints: Chemical energy in the battery converted into electrical energy
Electrical energy converted into light energy in the bulb
Some is also converted into heat energy, which is not useful for a torch
questions.whyMarksLost: Useful and wasted conversions are a distinct idea. The word energy must follow each form: chemical energy, electrical energy, light energy.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using where the energy came from and where it went.
questions.stimulus: A child on a swing is pushed once and then left alone. The swing goes lower and lower with each swing until it stops.
questions.stem: Explain why the swing eventually stops. Explain also why the total amount of energy has not decreased, even though the swing has stopped moving.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the energy is converted into heat energy and is no longer available to move the swing
friction and air resistance convert the swing's energy into heat energy

chain.text: The swing has kinetic energy as it moves and gravitational potential energy as it rises.
Friction at the pivot and air resistance act on the swing.
These convert some of its energy into heat energy on each swing.
Less energy remains for movement, so it swings lower each time until it stops.
The energy has not been destroyed; it is now heat energy in the surroundings.

questions.modelAnswer: After the push, the swing has kinetic energy as it moves and gravitational potential energy as it rises. As it swings, friction at the pivot and air resistance act on it, converting some of the swing's energy into heat energy on every swing. With less energy available for movement each time, the swing rises to a lower height until it stops. The total amount of energy has not decreased. Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another, so all the energy the swing began with is now heat energy spread through the pivot and the surrounding air.
markPoints: The swing has kinetic and gravitational potential energy
Friction and air resistance act on it
These convert some of its energy into heat energy
Less energy remains for movement, so it swings lower and stops
Energy is converted rather than destroyed, so the total is unchanged
questions.whyMarksLost: The energy is used up is marked wrong because it contradicts conservation. The final mark is for saying where the energy actually went.

questions.commandDemand: State the conversions in order for the whole chain.
questions.stimulus: A solar panel on a roof charges a battery during the day. At night the battery powers a fan.
questions.stem: Describe the energy conversions from the sun to the moving fan.

fuzzyTraps.precise: light energy from the sun is converted into electrical energy by the solar panel

chain.text: The solar panel converts light energy from the sun into electrical energy.
The battery stores this as chemical energy.
At night the chemical energy is converted back into electrical energy, and the fan converts it into kinetic energy.

questions.modelAnswer: The solar panel converts light energy from the sun into electrical energy. This electrical energy is stored in the battery as chemical energy. At night the chemical energy in the battery is converted back into electrical energy, which flows to the fan. The fan converts the electrical energy into kinetic energy as its blades turn, and some is also converted into sound energy and heat energy.
markPoints: Light energy converted into electrical energy by the solar panel
Electrical energy stored as chemical energy in the battery
Chemical energy converted back into electrical energy at night
Electrical energy converted into kinetic energy by the fan
questions.whyMarksLost: The battery step is skipped most often. A battery stores chemical energy; it does not store electricity.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the source of the energy.
questions.stem: Explain why the sun is described as the source of almost all the energy used by living things on Earth.

fuzzyTraps.precise: green plants convert light energy from the sun into stored energy in food

chain.text: Green plants absorb light energy from the sun.
During photosynthesis they convert it into stored energy in food.
This energy passes to animals along the food chain when they eat plants or other animals.

questions.modelAnswer: Green plants are producers. They absorb light energy from the sun and convert it into stored energy in the food they make during photosynthesis. When animals eat plants, this stored energy is transferred to them, and it passes further along the food chain when those animals are eaten. Almost all the energy used by living things can therefore be traced back to light energy from the sun.
markPoints: Green plants convert light energy from the sun into stored energy in food by photosynthesis
This energy is passed to animals along the food chain
questions.whyMarksLost: The link through the food chain is the second mark. Answers that stop at photosynthesis have explained plants but not living things in general.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and give the reason using energy stores.
questions.stimulus: Two identical balls are dropped onto the same hard floor. Ball A is dropped from 1 metre and Ball B from 2 metres.
questions.stem: Predict which ball will bounce higher and explain why. Explain also why neither ball bounces back to the height it was dropped from.

fuzzyTraps.vague: B is higher so it bounces more
fuzzyTraps.precise: B has more gravitational potential energy at the start, so it has more kinetic energy on impact

chain.text: Ball B will bounce higher.
Ball B starts higher, so it has more gravitational potential energy.
More is converted into kinetic energy as it falls, so it hits the floor with more energy.
At the bounce, some energy is converted into heat and sound energy, so less is left to raise it.

questions.modelAnswer: Ball B will bounce higher. Because Ball B is released from a greater height it has more gravitational potential energy at the start, and as it falls this is converted into kinetic energy, so it strikes the floor with more energy and more is available to be converted back into gravitational potential energy as it rebounds. Neither ball returns to its starting height because at the moment of impact some of its energy is converted into heat energy and sound energy, which is why a bounce can be heard. That energy is no longer available to lift the ball, so each bounce is lower than the one before.
markPoints: Ball B bounces higher
Greater starting height means more gravitational potential energy
Converted into more kinetic energy, so more energy at impact
Some energy is converted into heat and sound at the bounce, so it cannot return to full height
questions.whyMarksLost: The sound of the bounce is the clue the examiner plants. If you can hear it, energy has left the ball.

questions.commandDemand: Read the data and state the conclusion about efficiency, quoting figures.
questions.stimulus:
Two bulbs were each supplied with 100 units of electrical energy. The energy converted into light and into heat was measured.

Bulb X: 10 units of light energy, 90 units of heat energy
Bulb Y: 75 units of light energy, 25 units of heat energy
questions.stem: Infer which bulb is more useful for lighting a room, and explain your answer.

fuzzyTraps.vague: Y is better because it is brighter
fuzzyTraps.precise: Y converts a greater proportion of the electrical energy into light energy

chain.text: Bulb Y is more useful for lighting.
Y converts 75 of every 100 units into light energy, while X converts only 10.
Less of the electrical energy supplied to Y is converted into heat energy, which is not useful for lighting.

questions.modelAnswer: Bulb Y is more useful for lighting a room. For every 100 units of electrical energy supplied, Bulb Y converts 75 units into light energy while Bulb X converts only 10 units. Bulb X converts 90 units into heat energy, which is not useful for lighting the room. Bulb Y therefore converts a much greater proportion of the electrical energy supplied into the form that is wanted.
markPoints: Bulb Y chosen, with the light energy figures quoted
Y converts a greater proportion of electrical energy into light energy
X converts most of its electrical energy into heat energy, which is not useful for lighting
questions.whyMarksLost: An inference from a table that quotes no figures from the table loses a mark for missing evidence.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a workable change and explain it using energy conversion.
questions.stimulus: A toy car powered by a stretched rubber band travels only a short distance before stopping.
questions.stem: Suggest one change that would make the car travel further, and explain why it would work.

fuzzyTraps.vague: stretch the band more so it goes faster
fuzzyTraps.precise: stretching the band further stores more elastic potential energy, which is converted into more kinetic energy

chain.text: Stretch the rubber band further before releasing the car.
This stores more elastic potential energy in the band.
More elastic potential energy is converted into kinetic energy, so the car travels further before friction converts it all into heat energy.

questions.modelAnswer: The rubber band could be stretched further before the car is released. Stretching it further stores a greater amount of elastic potential energy in the band. When the car is released, more elastic potential energy is converted into kinetic energy, so the car moves off with more energy and travels a greater distance before friction converts all of that energy into heat energy and it stops.
markPoints: A workable change, such as stretching the band further or reducing friction
Explained using more elastic potential energy converted into more kinetic energy
questions.whyMarksLost: Naming the store as elastic potential energy is the mark. 'The band has more power' uses an everyday word where a scientific one is required.
